prompt.context: Our client is a steel manufacturing company in the Netherlands. They are considering investing in an advanced analytics tool that will help them better predict inventory schedule. They are also looking at immediate methods to save costs.
prompt.question: A) Steel coils are currently transported from the factory to customers via Railways, Trucks, Vessels and Barges. Analyze these four transport methods and suggest any opportunities for cost saving. B) Suggest any alternative techniques to save cost in the immediate future.

clarifying_info.q: How many countries does the client operate in?
clarifying_info.a: The client operates internationally in 100+ countries.
Customers are predominantly large B2B manufacturers with both short and long-term contracts.

clarifying_info.q: What products does the client ship?
clarifying_info.a: For this case, assume steel is only manufactured and shipped as coils.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a specific cost-saving target?
clarifying_info.a: No specific target; the objective is to identify cost-saving opportunities.

exhibits.title: Transport Methods Overview
exhibits.shows: A table comparing four transport modes (Rail, Truck, Barge, Vessel) across five dimensions: Deliveries per week, Volume per delivery (tons), Utilization %, Cost per ton ($), and Frequency (days between deliveries).

exhibits.title: Transfer of Goods from Pier to Trucks
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the number of steel coils transferred from pier to trucks over 21 weeks. Total volume for delivery is stated as 5,700 steel coils; 1 steel coil = 10 tons. The chart shows elevated coil transfers in weeks 1 and 2, tapering off in later weeks.

framework: Cover both parts of the prompt: (A) four transport mode analysis for capacity/cost and (B) alternative immediate cost-saving techniques
Incorporate steel industry specifics (heavy industrial goods, international B2B, coil format)
Analyze costs: start with a profitability lens but focus narrowly on cost reduction as the prompt directs
For each transport mode evaluate: current utilization, cost per ton, weekly volume, and idle capacity that can be eliminated or consolidated
Identify cross-mode substitution opportunities (e.g., shift volume from high-cost to low-cost modes)
For Part B, brainstorm levers beyond transport: procurement, production scheduling, inventory management, contract renegotiation, KPI redesign

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the weekly cost for each transport mode and the potential cost savings if each mode ran at 100% utilization.
questions.guidance: Candidate should derive: (A) weekly volume = deliveries/week × volume/delivery; (B) weekly cost = weekly volume × cost/ton; (C) savings potential = weekly cost × (1 − utilization %). Strong candidates note that Rail and Truck have the largest absolute savings, and that Vessel at 100% utilization has zero capacity-driven savings. Candidate should question why truck usage is so high — this leads to Exhibit 2.

math.setup: For each mode: Volume/week (C) = A × B; Cost/week (F) = C × E; Savings potential (G) = F × (1 − D)
math.answer: $7.3M per week in potential savings through better capacity utilization across Rail ($3.3M), Truck ($3M), and Barge ($1M).

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, analyze why goods are being transferred from pier to trucks. Quantify the cost saving if this is corrected.
questions.guidance: Vessels run every 14 days but trucks run daily — when a vessel departs and leaves coils behind on the pier, those coils are shifted to trucks (high cost). Candidate should read the chart: weeks 1–2 show ~3,000 coils going to trucks; from week 3 onwards the pier-to-truck flow drops, suggesting a one-time overhang or that the first vessel departure left 3,000 coils behind. The remaining (5,700 − 3,000) = 2,700 coils could be redirected to avoid truck use. An excellent candidate notes that vessels run at 100% utilization (KPI-driven), which causes coils to be left behind; relaxing the KPI to 95% would reduce stranding.

math.setup: Cost saving = coils redirected away from trucks × weight per coil × (cost/ton truck − cost/ton vessel)
math.answer: $540,000 in additional savings from better inventory management to avoid pier-to-truck transfers.

questions.prompt: What is the total cost-saving potential identified in this case?
questions.guidance: Candidate should sum both identified savings streams: capacity optimization ($7.3M) and inventory management for vessels ($540K).

math.setup: Total = capacity utilization savings + inventory management savings

brainstorming.prompt: Part B: Beyond optimizing the four transport modes, what alternative techniques could the client use to reduce costs in the immediate future?

categories.name: Procurement & Sourcing
ideas: Renegotiate cost-per-ton rates with carriers given volume commitments
Consolidate carrier contracts to gain leverage

categories.name: Capacity & Scheduling
ideas: Reduce number of trucks deployed as utilization improves
Optimize delivery schedules to batch shipments and improve load factors
Use advanced analytics tool to better predict demand and align shipment timing

categories.name: Inventory Management
ideas: Reduce safety stock held at warehouses to lower carrying costs
Improve pier-to-vessel sequencing so fewer coils miss vessel departures
Implement better demand forecasting to avoid last-minute truck dispatches

categories.name: KPI & Contract Redesign
ideas: Change vessel KPI from 100% utilization to 95% to allow scheduling buffer and reduce pier overflow
Introduce on-time-in-full metrics that balance utilization with delivery reliability

categories.name: Modal Substitution
ideas: Shift volume from truck (highest cost/ton) to rail, barge, or vessel wherever routes allow
Evaluate if any truck routes overlap with rail/barge corridors

recommendation: Drive total cost savings of approximately $7.84M: $7.3M through better capacity utilization across Rail, Truck, and Barge, and $540K from improved inventory management that reduces pier-to-truck transfers
Continue investment in the advanced analytics tool to improve inventory scheduling, which directly addresses the identified cost driver of misaligned shipment timing
risks: Utilization assumptions may not hold if average figures mask wide variation across routes or seasons
Truck drivers may be unionized; reducing the truck fleet may require contract renegotiation and could face labor pushback
Vessel KPI changes require stakeholder alignment and may initially reduce throughput before gains are realized
next_steps: Modify vessel labor KPIs to target 95% utilization (instead of 100%) to reduce coils stranded at the pier
Gradually reduce the number of trucks deployed to improve per-vehicle utilization toward 100%
Renegotiate cost-per-ton rates with carriers once utilization data supports volume commitments
Accelerate implementation of the advanced analytics tool for inventory scheduling
